newsitem.title: LEBANON: Beirut bourse to have new listings, trade debt.
newsitem.headline: Beirut bourse to have new listings, trade debt.

text.p: The head of the Beirut Stock Exchange said on Friday the 18-month-old bourse would increase its share listings and add debt trading by the end of the year.

Gabriel Sehnaoui told Reuters the additional listings would add dynamism to the BSE and attract foreign investors seeking opportunities in the "underinvested Middle East markets". He would not identify the companies.
"I think that at the end of 1997, we will have around 15 companies which have their products listed. We will also have debt of companies and funds listed by then," he said.
Beirut financiers believe the bourse's solid infrastructure, the country's liberal economy and an enhanced post-war image would help the BSE become a leading regional market.
Ziad Makkawi, head of capital markets for the Beirut finance house Middle East Capital Group, said new instruments were being readied for domestic listing at the end of this month.
"There are deals being worked right now on the market that involve securitization transactions, floating-rate notes and a variety of other types of instruments," Makkawi said.
Despite having only eight companies listed, the BSE has grown strongly since reopening in January 1996 after a 13-year gap caused by Lebanon's civil war.
MECG was lead manager for domestic offerings by Banque Libanaise pour le Commerce in December and Bank of Beirut in April. Banque Audi was listed in January.
Those banks have led the market up in 1997, increasing by 93 percent, 174 percent and 87 percent respectively over their issue prices.
"We began with only 3,000 shares being exchanged every day and with a volume of $300,000. Now we have a daily turnover of around 300,000 shares for $4 million," Sehnaoui said.
Brokers on the BSE floor believe demand is shifting from bank stocks into Solidere, Lebanon's biggest company, which has recently started dominating market activity.
Solidere A and B shares traded at $13 on Friday. The company's global depositary receipts, however, traded at $16.9 in London -- 30 percent above the underlying shares in Beirut.
"There is hardly any analyst either domestic or international who does not believe that there is much value in the stock, that it is undervalued really," Makkawi said.

On August 22, shareholders in the $1.98 billion real estate company rebuilding war-ravaged Beirut will vote on lifting ownership restrictions to let foreign investors and local institutions buy shares.

"All the institutional money that is out in the United States, Europe and the Far East is now going to be able to have access to what is undoubtedly the most undervalued stock in Lebanon," Makkawi said.
"This will give a great impetus to the BSE. It will give it greater visibility," he added.

The U.S. decision last Wednesday to lift a 10-year-old ban on its citizens visiting Lebanon should help. "This also will encourage international funds to come to the BSE. It is very important because the biggest funds are now American and they are moving into emerging markets," Sehnaoui said.
But, he said, Middle East peace was the key to a prosperous Lebanese financial market. "If there is peace, there will be big activity. We hope we will be the leaders," he said.
